The Longest Afternoon at Kestrel Park

MARCUS HALLOWAY, STILL in his warmups, leans on the dugout rail and watches the grounds crew drag the infield in slow overlapping circles, the way he watched them as a boy from the bleachers behind the visitors' bullpen.

But Halloway is 20.

He watches clips on his phone between innings, the same three plays over and again, each one a small argument with himself about where his hands were and whether the ball ever had a chance of staying fair at all.

Halloway waits in the tunnel before the eighth inning. Getty Images

THERE IS ONLY ONE way to learn whether a player that age can carry a season, and that is to hand him the season and stand well back, which is more or less what the club has decided to do this September.

A young infielder takes grounders at dusk. Reuters

The catcher who learned to hit at 28

BY THE TIME Halloway turned 20, his mother had driven him to four states for tournaments that started before sunrise and finished in parking lots lit by the headlights of idling minivans.

Halloway signs a ball for a boy along the third-base line. Courtesy of the Halloway family
